title: Unveiling and Characterising Ubiquitous Nitrogen Enhancement in $6 \leq z \leq 10$ Galaxies with JWST Spectroscopy
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a growing number of $z>6$ galaxies with enhanced N/O ratios that challenge standard chemical enrichment frameworks. We test whether this is exclusive to extreme systems or a generic feature of $6 \leq z \leq 10$ populations through a stacking analysis of 135 galaxies with JWST/NIRSpec $R\sim1000$ spectroscopy, probing the origin of N, C and O enrichment and its dependence on recent star formation. A full-sample composite reveals prominent C III], C IV, N IV] and He II emission, demonstrating a ubiquity of high-ionisation UV lines. Auroral [O III]$λ$4363 electron temperatures and multi-ionisation zone modelling yield direct-$T_e$ abundances with supersolar $\log(\mathrm{N/O}) = -0.57^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and subsolar $\log(\mathrm{C/O}) = -0.80^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$ at $12 + \log(\mathrm{O/H}) = 7.79^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$, in contrast with local samples and suggesting significant nitrogen enhancement within the first billion years. Stacking further by recent star formation activity over burst timescales of $Δt = 3$--$20$~Myr, we find that sources caught in a recent burst are less enriched in both N/O and metallicity than those in a relative lull, with the largest contrasts confined to the shortest timescales. C/O, however, remains largely invariant across all metrics. We interpret these observations as the result of delayed AGB enrichment across multiple burst episodes, together with dilution by pristine gas inflows. Cosmological simulations reproduce this trend with CCSNe and AGB yields alone, without the need for shorter-lived (super-)massive stars. Enhanced N/O therefore appears to be a generic feature of high-redshift systems, produced by standard enrichment processes rather than requiring new physical frameworks.

AI.tldr: A stacking analysis of 135 z~6-10 galaxies with JWST/NIRSpec reveals ubiquitous high-ionization UV lines and supersolar N/O with subsolar C/O, explained by delayed AGB enrichment plus pristine gas dilution across burst cycles—requiring no exotic stellar populations.
AI.motivation: JWST has uncovered z>6 galaxies with enhanced N/O ratios that defy standard chemical enrichment models, but it is unclear whether such enhancement is exclusive to extreme systems or generic to all high-redshift populations, and whether new physical frameworks are required to explain it.
AI.method: Stacking analysis of 135 galaxies with JWST/NIRSpec R~1000 spectroscopy, using auroral [O III] λ4363 electron temperatures and multi-ionization zone modelling for direct-T_e abundances, with further stacking by recent star formation activity over burst timescales of Δt = 3-20 Myr, and comparison with cosmological simulations using CCSNe and AGB yields.
AI.result: The full-sample composite shows prominent C III], C IV, N IV] and He II emission, with supersolar log(N/O) = -0.57 and subsolar log(C/O) = -0.80 at 12+log(O/H) = 7.79. Sources in recent bursts are less enriched in N/O and metallicity than quiescent ones, with largest contrasts at shortest timescales, while C/O remains invariant. Cosmological simulations reproduce this trend with standard CCSNe and AGB yields alone.
AI.conclusion: Enhanced N/O is a generic feature of high-redshift z~6-10 systems rather than exclusive to extreme objects, produced by delayed AGB enrichment across multiple burst episodes combined with pristine gas dilution—standard enrichment processes suffice without invoking shorter-lived (super-)massive stars.

title: A cosmic collision in the making: JWST/NIRISS reveals a merging and maturing protocluster core at z~3 around a red quasar
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 18 pages, 10 figures, including a 5-page appendix with 3 figures
summary: We report the discovery of ``The Step'', a dense protocluster at z=3 revealed by JWST/NIRISS Wide-Field Slitless Spectroscopy (WFSS) of the field around the luminous quasar and starburst SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3. The protocluster contains at least 18 member galaxies and exhibits two substructures in the 3D position-velocity space - notably a distinctive step-like distribution, from which the nickname derives. We propose that the Step may be undergoing a merger of two haloes, which could also explain the large velocity span (700-850km/s) between galaxies along the densest line of sight. This sightline contains seven galaxies within 70 projected kpc from the quasar, consistent with a remarkably dense protocluster core. We derive a galaxy overdensity of a factor >100 in the core and >15 within 1 Mpc$^2$, making it one of the densest structures known at this redshift, and a very massive halo of $13.1 < log M_{\rm halo}/ M_\odot < 13.8$, which suggests the structure could potentially evolve into a massive, Coma-like cluster at z=0. Compared to the field, the star-forming galaxies in the Step show slightly elevated levels of star formation. Yet, we find two quiescent galaxies with strong D4000 breaks and no evidence for ongoing star formation. Compared to other z=3 protoclusters, the Step exhibits similar or slightly suppressed star-forming activity. We also identify two new AGN candidates and find tentative evidence for an enhanced AGN fraction (10-20%) compared to the field. The protocluster constitutes one of the emerging handful of maturing structures at 2 < z < 4 that host both star-forming and quenched galaxies. This redshift regime may thus be a key transitional epoch for cluster studies, where overdensities transition from being the most active sites of star formation in the early Universe towards shaping the massive passive ellipticals seen in the cores of today's clusters.

AI.tldr: Discovery of "The Step," a dense protocluster at z=3 found via JWST/NIRISS spectroscopy around the quasar SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3. It contains at least 18 members with a distinctive step-like distribution in 3D position-velocity space, suggesting a merger of two haloes. The structure exhibits an extreme galaxy overdensity (>100 in the core), a very massive halo (log M_halo/M_sun = 13.1-13.8), elevated star formation, two quiescent galaxies, and an enhanced AGN fraction, and may evolve into a Coma-like cluster at z=0.
AI.motivation: To uncover and characterize massive protoclusters at z=3, a key transitional epoch where high-density structures transition from the most active star-forming sites to the progenitors of massive passive cluster ellipticals seen in today's clusters.
AI.method: Using JWST/NIRISS Wide-Field Slitless Spectroscopy (WFSS) to obtain redshifts of galaxies in the field around the luminous quasar and starburst SDSSJ165202.64+172852.3, enabling 3D position-velocity mapping of the protocluster, measuring overdensities, halo mass estimates, star formation properties (via D4000 breaks and star-forming activity), and identifying AGN candidates.
AI.result: Found a protocluster with at least 18 members forming a step-like distribution in velocity space, consistent with two merging haloes. The structure shows a galaxy overdensity of factor >100 in the core and >15 within 1 Mpc^2, a massive halo of 13.1 < log M_halo < 13.8, seven galaxies within 70 projected kpc of the quasar, slightly elevated star formation relative to the field but comparable to other z=3 protoclusters, two quiescent galaxies with strong D4000 breaks, and an enhanced AGN fraction (10-20%).
AI.conclusion: The Step is one of the densest known structures at z=3 and among the handful of maturing protoclusters at 2 < z < 4 hosting both star-forming and quenched galaxies. It may evolve into a massive, Coma-like cluster at z=0, and this redshift regime represents a key transitional epoch for cluster formation studies.

title: Flat Galactic Rotation Curves Interpreted as Evidence for the Mach's Principle
comment: Submitted. Comments welcome to aescala@das.uchile.cl
summary:
We explore the possibility of a Machian interpretation for the phenomena associated with asymptotically flat rotation curves in disk galaxies, providing an alternative to both the Lambda-Cold Dark Matter ($Λ$CDM) paradigm and MOdified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). We argue that the MOND acceleration scale $a_0$ is likely not a new fundamental constant, but rather a manifestation of the cosmological scales of the observable Universe ($a_0 \sim c^2/R_u \sim c^4/GM_u \sim c/t_u$). We rewrite the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation (BTFR) in a cosmological format, $\frac{M_{\rm bar}}{M_{u}} = \left( \frac{V}{c} \right)^4$, suggesting that the transition to the non-Newtonian regime occurs when local accelerations become small enough to feel the global cosmic boundary, and showing that any Machian interpretation must fulfill a relation of this form. Furthermore, this framework naturally predicts a cosmological evolution of the BTFR normalization as the mass in the observable Universe evolves. We test these predictions against recent high-redshift observations ($z \sim 2$ and $z \sim 5$), finding that the data
  favor a flat, baryon-only, $Λ$-dominated quasi-de Sitter universe ($Ω_m \approx 0.05$, $Ω_Λ\approx 0.95$) over standard MOND or $Λ$CDM parameters. These results suggest that flat galactic rotation curves may be interpreted as compelling evidence in favor of Mach's Principle, in at least some of its versions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Machian interpretation for asymptotically flat rotation curves in disk galaxies as an alternative to both ΛCDM and MOND, arguing that the MOND acceleration scale a0 is a manifestation of cosmological scales rather than a new fundamental constant, and showing that the BTFR written in cosmological form predicts a cosmological evolution of its normalization that is favored by high-redshift observations.
AI.motivation: The authors seek a third alternative to the standard ΛCDM paradigm and MOND for explaining flat galactic rotation curves, motivated by the possibility that the MOND acceleration scale is not a fundamental constant but rather reflects global cosmological scales, thereby connecting local galactic dynamics to Mach's Principle.
AI.method: The authors rewrite the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation in cosmological form (M_bar/M_u = (V/c)^4), relate the MOND acceleration scale to cosmological quantities (a0 ~ c^2/R_u ~ c^4/GM_u ~ c/t_u), and test the framework's prediction of BTFR normalization evolution against high-redshift observational data at z~2 and z~5.
AI.result: The high-redshift data favor a flat, baryon-only, Λ-dominated quasi-de Sitter universe (Ω_m ≈ 0.05, Ω_Λ ≈ 0.95) over standard MOND or ΛCDM parameters, providing observational support for the Machian framework.
AI.conclusion: Flat galactic rotation curves may be compelling evidence in favor of Mach's Principle (in at least some versions), with the transition to the non-Newtonian regime occurring when local accelerations are small enough to feel the global cosmic boundary.

title: Discovery of four Narrow-line Type-1 Quasars at z = 2.54 -- 6.06 with Subaru 'Onohi'ula PFS-SSP
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, submitted to PASJ
summary: We report the discovery of four narrow-line type-1 quasars (NLQ1s) from the Subaru 'Onohi'ula Prime Focus Spectrograph Subaru Strategic Program (PFS-SSP). To extend a comprehensive understanding of this population to the distant universe, we searched for broad-line AGNs (quasars) whose rest-UV spectral shapes resemble those of local NLS1 galaxies, utilizing the Ly$α$ line profile. We identified four NLQ1s, including one candidate, at $z=2.54$ -- $6.06$. The obtained spectra show a prominent Ly$α$ emission line with a very low continuum level. The measured full width at half maximum (FWHM) of Ly$α$ ranges from $1410 \ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ to $1510 \ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ with a mean of $\sim 1430 \,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Although we used only line width information for the NLQ1 selection, the resulting equivalent widths (EW) of Ly$α$ are higher (the mean $\sim 190$\,Å\ in the rest frame) than the typical values of quasars. Two quasars have exceptionally large Ly$α$ luminosity, accounting for $\sim 3$ -- $4$\% of the bolometric luminosity. We measured black hole masses and Eddington ratios for three objects whose C\,\textsc{iv} line is available. The resulting black hole masses are $\sim 10^{6.9}$ -- $10^{7.7}\, M_{\odot}$ with high Eddington ratios ($> 0.1$), consistent with those of NLS1 galaxies reported in the low-$z$ universe. N\,\textsc{v} and C\,\textsc{iv} broad absorption lines are detected in one object. This quasar can be classified as a mini-BAL quasar, which further supports the idea that this NLQ1 is indeed a luminous version of an NLS1 galaxy.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of four narrow-line type-1 quasars (NLQ1s) at redshift z=2.54–6.06 from the Subaru PFS-SSP survey. These objects were identified by searching for broad-line AGNs whose rest-UV spectral shapes resemble local NLS1 galaxies using Lyα line profiles. The quasars show narrow Lyα FWHM (~1410–1510 km/s), high equivalent widths (~190 Å), and low continuum levels. Black hole masses (~10^6.9–10^7.7 M⊙) and high Eddington ratios (>0.1) are consistent with local NLS1s, confirming these are luminous distant counterparts of NLS1 galaxies. One object exhibits N V and C IV broad absorption lines, classifying it as a mini-BAL quasar.
AI.motivation: To extend the comprehensive understanding of narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) galaxies to the distant universe, since the local NLS1 population has been well-studied but their high-redshift counterparts are largely unexplored.
AI.method: Searched for broad-line AGNs (quasars) whose rest-UV spectral shapes resemble local NLS1 galaxies, using Lyα line profiles. Selected candidates based on Lyα line width measurements and followed up with Subaru PFS-SSP spectroscopy.
AI.result: Identified four NLQ1s at z=2.54–6.06 with Lyα FWHM of 1410–1510 km/s, high EW (~190 Å), and low continuum. Black hole masses of ~10^6.9–10^7.7 M⊙ with Eddington ratios >0.1. One object shows mini-BAL features in N V and C IV.
AI.conclusion: These NLQ1s are luminous high-redshift counterparts of local NLS1 galaxies, supported by similar black hole masses, Eddington ratios, and the presence of a mini-BAL object, extending the NLS1 population to z~6.

title: The Last Crossing in Excursion-Set Theory of Cosmic Reionization
summary: I introduce the last crossing of the photon-counting barrier as a statistic for analytical models of cosmic reionization. Because ionizing galaxies are biased tracers of density and their photons propagate through gas of spatially varying opacity, the galaxy-IGM connection requires statistics beyond the global ionized fraction. The excursion-set model of Furlanetto et al. (2004) identifies the ionized-bubble scale around a point with the first crossing of a photon-counting barrier. I develop the last-crossing formalism and define the last-crossing scale, $R_\ell$, as the smallest scale on which the enclosed photon budget still ionizes the enclosed gas. I derive its distribution analytically. Using the empirical-barrier framework of Kaurov (2016) applied to CROC simulations, I measure both crossings in the simulated IGM. The last-crossing formalism separates externally ionized regions, whose photon-counting condition fails below $R_\ell$, from internally ionized regions whose trajectories remain above the barrier to the resolution scale. Resolved external regions are predominantly underdense, with larger $R_\ell$ selecting lower density and later reionization. At fixed local density, first-crossing scale, and reionization redshift, these regions show deficits in ionizing-luminosity and galaxy-number density at small radius relative to matched unresolved regions, and excesses in both at intermediate radius. Their combination of low gas density and a deficit of nearby sources suggests that Ly$α$ transmission spikes may preferentially arise in these regions: low density reduces the opacity, while sources on larger scales maintain the ionized state. The last-crossing picture connects the internal source geometry of ionized regions to a testable prediction for radial galaxy distributions around transmission-selected IGM locations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "last crossing of the photon-counting barrier" as a new statistic for analytical models of cosmic reionization, complementing the first-crossing formalism of Furlanetto et al. (2004). The last-crossing scale Rℓ is defined as the smallest scale where the enclosed photon budget still ionizes the gas. Using both analytical derivations and CROC simulation measurements, the formalism separates externally ionized (predominantly underdense) regions from internally ionized ones, and predicts that Lyα transmission spikes may preferentially arise in low-density regions with a deficit of nearby sources but sufficient sources at larger scales.
AI.motivation: The galaxy-IGM connection during reionization requires statistics beyond the global ionized fraction because ionizing galaxies are biased tracers of density and their photons propagate through gas with spatially varying opacity. The existing excursion-set first-crossing formalism identifies ionized-bubble scales but is insufficient to characterize the full galaxy-IGM relationship.
AI.method: The author develops the last-crossing formalism analytically, defining Rℓ as the smallest scale on which the enclosed photon budget still ionizes the gas, deriving its distribution analytically. The framework is applied to CROC simulations using the empirical-barrier framework of Kaurov (2016), measuring both first- and last-crossing scales in the simulated IGM.
AI.result: The last-crossing formalism separates externally ionized regions (whose photon-counting condition fails below Rℓ) from internally ionized regions (trajectories stay above the barrier to resolution scale). Resolved external regions are predominantly underdense, with larger Rℓ selecting lower density and later reionization. At fixed local density, first-crossing scale, and reionization redshift, these regions show deficits in ionizing luminosity and galaxy-number density at small radius vs matched unresolved regions, with excesses at intermediate radius.
AI.conclusion: The combination of low gas density and a deficit of nearby sources suggests Lyα transmission spikes may preferentially arise in externally ionized low-density regions, where low density reduces opacity while sources on larger scales maintain ionization. This connects internal source geometry of ionized regions to testable predictions for radial galaxy distributions around transmission-selected IGM locations.

title: An X-ray Absorption-Line Survey of the Circumgalactic Medium of M31 with XMM-Newton
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ. 13 pages, 5 figures, and 3 tables
summary: X-ray absorption line spectroscopy provides a powerful method for probing the extended hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) of individual galaxies. In this study, we present the first survey of \osv and \oeit absorption lines toward the hot halo of M\,31, using $15$ and $18$ background active galactic nuclei, with impact parameters ranging from $R_{\rm imp}\sim300$--$730$~kpc and $\sim190$--$730$~kpc, respectively. We find a marginal excess absorption above the expected Milky Way (MW) foreground toward the innermost sightlines, consistent with an additional hot-CGM contribution associated with M\,31. Comparing sightlines inside and outside $R_{\rm imp}=300$--$350$~kpc, the excess corresponds to a mean equivalent width of $\sim4$--$9$~mÅ for the inner \osv sightlines at $R_{\rm imp}\sim310$~kpc and $\sim17$~mÅ for the inner \oeit sightlines at $R_{\rm imp}\sim200$~kpc, with a nominal combined significance level of $2.2$--$2.3\,σ$. The hot-CGM mass inferred from this excess is highly model dependent, especially on the assumed CGM boundary, and therefore does not yet provide a robust baryon census. Attributing the excess entirely to hot gas confined within approximately the virial radius of M\,31 would require a CGM mass exceeding the nominal ``missing'' baryon budget. The inferred mass decreases to a few $\times10^{11}~M_\odot$ when the assumed CGM boundary is extended to $400-500$~kpc. Deeper observations, both through longer exposures of existing sightlines and the inclusion of additional inner-halo targets, will be essential to robustly constrain the properties of the hot CGM of M\,31.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first spectroscopic survey of O VII and O VIII absorption lines probing the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) of M31 using 15 and 18 background AGN sightlines at impact parameters of 190–730 kpc. A marginal excess absorption (2.2–2.3σ combined) is detected toward the inner sightlines, but the inferred hot-CGM mass is highly model-dependent and does not yet provide a robust baryon census.
AI.motivation: To probe the extended hot circumgalactic medium of M31 using X-ray absorption line spectroscopy, which provides a powerful tool for studying individual galaxies' hot halos and addressing the missing baryon problem.
AI.method: Used X-ray absorption line spectroscopy of O VII and O VIII toward 15 and 18 background AGNs respectively, with impact parameters from ~190–730 kpc, comparing inner sightlines against Milky Way foreground expectations.
AI.result: A marginal excess absorption above the MW foreground is found toward the innermost sightlines, corresponding to mean equivalent widths of ~4–9 mÅ (O VII at R~310 kpc) and ~17 mÅ (O VIII at R~200 kpc), with combined significance of 2.2–2.3σ. The inferred CGM mass is highly model-dependent, ranging from exceeding the missing baryon budget if confined to the virial radius, down to a few ×10¹¹ M☉ if the boundary extends to 400–500 kpc.
AI.conclusion: The current data provide only marginal evidence for a hot M31 CGM and do not yet yield a robust baryon census. Deeper observations and additional inner-halo sightlines are required to robustly constrain the hot CGM properties of M31.

title: Lyman Break Galaxy selection and redshift measurement with supervised contrastive learning
comment: 36 pages, 15 figures, submitted to JCAP
summary: Some of the next steps for high-precision cosmology lie within the high-redshift, high-density universe. Spectroscopic survey experiments such as the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI)'s second phase DESI Run 2 will shift towards probing Lyman Break Galaxy (LBG) populations from z$\sim$2 to z$\sim$4.5. For this faint sample, spectroscopic redshift measurement and sample decontamination remains a challenge, even after target selection. We propose an approach based on supervised weighted contrastive learning, in order to both learn a redshift representation for spectra and decontaminate the sample from quasars and low redshift emission line galaxies. This strategy generalizes the contrastive learning loss approach with continuous relationship weights, such that the network simultaneously learns redshift and classification tasks. The model shows stronger outlier classification and comparable redshift identification performances when compared to the previous network used for DESI (a modified version of QuasarNET) on the same dataset. In particular, contrastive learning is well suited to the small, visually-inspected sample used for training and testing, especially given the multi-task nature of this work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a supervised weighted contrastive learning approach to simultaneously learn redshift representations and decontaminate spectroscopic samples from quasars and low-redshift emission line galaxies for high-redshift LBG surveys (e.g., DESI Run 2). The method outperforms the previous QuasarNET-based network on outlier classification while achieving comparable redshift identification performance.
AI.motivation: Upcoming high-redshift, high-density cosmology surveys (like DESI Run 2) targeting Lyman Break Galaxies from z~2 to z~4.5 face challenges in spectroscopic redshift measurement and sample decontamination due to faint samples. Existing approaches struggle with multi-task learning (redshift estimation plus classification) on small, visually-inspected training datasets.
AI.method: A supervised weighted contrastive learning framework that generalizes the standard contrastive learning loss with continuous relationship weights. The network simultaneously learns a redshift representation for spectra and performs classification to decontaminate the sample from quasars and low-redshift emission line galaxies. The model is trained and tested on the same visually-inspected DESI dataset used for prior work.
AI.result: The proposed model demonstrates stronger outlier classification performance and comparable redshift identification accuracy when compared to the modified QuasarNET baseline used for DESI on the same dataset. Contrastive learning proves well-suited for the small training sample and the multi-task nature of the problem.
AI.conclusion: Supervised weighted contrastive learning is an effective strategy for joint redshift estimation and sample decontamination in high-redshift spectroscopic surveys, particularly benefiting from multi-task learning on limited but visually-inspected training data for next-generation cosmology experiments.

title: Spiral Morphology and Radial Migration: Kinematically heating, cooling, and cold
comment: 10 figures, 2 tables
summary: Transient spiral arms are known to drive radial redistribution of stars and thus could play a central role in shaping disk galaxies, including modifying, over time, the age, chemical, and kinematic (chrono-chemo-dynamic) distributions in the Milky Way. However, the physical factors governing the efficiency of such processes remain poorly understood. This paper investigates how the morphology of spiral arms -- the number, pitch angle, lifetime, and radial dependence of the pattern speed -- influences orbital redistribution through 'cold torquing' at the corotation resonance(s). Analytic expressions are derived for the maximum radial excursion of stars trapped at corotation that explicitly account for spiral morphology, predicting that the efficiency of cold torquing for a density-wave like spiral is greater for more open spiral patterns. Tracer-particle simulations confirm the analytic prediction, in both two- and three-dimensional galactic potentials. In contrast, spirals that have a radially dependent pattern speed such that they corotate with the disk at all radii exhibit the opposite behavior, with cold torquing becoming more efficient as the spiral winds to smaller pitch angles over time. This study further finds that resonant interactions from the same transient spiral causing cold torquing naturally also produces both kinematic heating and cooling of orbits away from corotation. These results demonstrate that spiral morphology alone cannot predict the efficiency of cold torquing and suggest that the relationship between spiral pitch angle and radial redistribution provides a potential diagnostic for distinguishing between competing theories of spiral structure.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how spiral arm morphology (number, pitch angle, lifetime, and pattern speed radial dependence) influences orbital redistribution via 'cold torquing' at corotation resonances. Analytic expressions predict that more open density-wave spiral patterns produce more efficient cold torquing, confirmed by tracer-particle simulations in 2D and 3D potentials. Conversely, spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds that corotate everywhere show opposite behavior, becoming more efficient as pitch angles wind tighter. Resonant interactions also cause both heating and cooling away from corotation, and the pitch angle–redistribution relation could serve as a diagnostic between competing spiral structure theories.
AI.motivation: Transient spiral arms can drive radial redistribution of stars and shape disk galaxies' chrono-chemo-dynamic distributions over time, but the physical factors governing the efficiency of these processes, particularly the role of spiral morphology, are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors derive analytic expressions for the maximum radial excursion of stars trapped at corotation that explicitly depend on spiral morphology (number, pitch angle, lifetime, and pattern speed radial profile). They then validate these predictions using tracer-particle simulations in both two- and three-dimensional galactic potentials, comparing density-wave-like spirals against spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds.
AI.result: For density-wave-like spirals, cold torquing efficiency increases with more open pitch angles, as predicted analytically. For spirals with radially dependent pattern speeds corotating at all radii, the opposite trend holds: efficiency increases as the spiral winds to smaller pitch angles. The same transient spiral also produces both kinematic heating and cooling of orbits away from corotation.
AI.conclusion: Spiral morphology alone cannot uniquely predict cold torquing efficiency; the relationship between pitch angle and radial redistribution offers a potential observational diagnostic to distinguish between competing theories of spiral structure in disk galaxies.

title: Reconstructing Dark Matter Mass and Discriminating Standard and Non-Standard WIMP-Nucleus Interactions with Paleo-Detectors
comment: 27 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables
summary: Paleo-detectors record and retain crystal damage in ancient minerals from nuclear recoils induced by dark matter scattering over geological timescales. Previous studies have shown that paleo-detectors can provide sensitivity to a variety of dark matter (DM) scenarios which is complementary to conventional direct-detection experiments. In this paper, we complete the first detailed study of how well paleo-detectors can reconstruct DM parameters or distinguish between different types of DM interactions with nuclei in the presence of a DM signal, considering both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleus scattering. For representative nuclear recoil track read-out scenarios, we demonstrate that weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) DM masses can be reconstructed for a variety of Non-Relativistic Effective Field Theory (NREFT) interactions between WIMPs and nuclei. In particular, paleo-detectors are projected to be capable of reconstructing WIMP masses $\lesssim$ 10 GeV, a regime that is challenging for conventional direct-detection experiments; further, we find that paleo-detectors could reconstruct WIMP masses up to 1 TeV for hypothetical signals within their accessible parameter space, extending the mass range over which reconstruction is possible by up to a factor of $\sim 2$ compared with analogous studies of conventional direct-detection experiments. In addition, we demonstrate that paleo-detectors could discriminate between canonical spin-independent or spin-dependent NREFT interactions and non-canonical interactions which can depend on the relative velocity or momentum transferred between the WIMP and nucleus. Specifically, at WIMP masses $\gtrsim$ 10 GeV, we project that canonical NREFT interactions can be excluded by paleo-detectors in the cases of nearly all non-canonical interactions without measurement of nuclear recoil direction, which conventional experiments typically require.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first detailed study of how well paleo-detectors (ancient minerals recording crystal damage from dark matter recoils over geological timescales) can reconstruct dark matter parameters and distinguish between different DM interaction types, considering both elastic and inelastic scattering. They demonstrate WIMP mass reconstruction for various NREFT interactions, especially for masses ≤10 GeV (challenging for conventional detectors) and up to 1 TeV, and show discrimination between canonical and non-canonical DM-nucleus interactions without requiring nuclear recoil direction measurements.
AI.motivation: Previous studies established that paleo-detectors offer sensitivity to various DM scenarios complementary to conventional direct-detection experiments. However, no detailed study had been performed on how well paleo-detectors could reconstruct DM parameters or discriminate between different types of DM-nucleus interactions in the presence of a signal—this gap motivates the present work.
AI.method: The study considers representative nuclear recoil track read-out scenarios for paleo-detectors and analyzes both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleus scattering within the Non-Relativistic Effective Field Theory (NREFT) framework. They perform parameter reconstruction for WIMP masses and assess the ability to discriminate between canonical spin-independent/spin-dependent interactions and non-canonical interactions that depend on relative velocity or momentum transfer.
AI.result: Paleo-detectors can reconstruct WIMP masses ≤10 GeV (a regime challenging for conventional experiments) and up to 1 TeV for hypothetical signals, extending the reconstruction mass range by up to ~2× compared to analogous conventional direct-detection studies. For WIMP masses ≥10 GeV, canonical NREFT interactions can be excluded in nearly all non-canonical interaction cases without requiring nuclear recoil direction measurements—something conventional experiments typically need.
AI.conclusion: Paleo-detectors offer significant advantages over conventional direct-detection experiments for DM parameter reconstruction and interaction-type discrimination, particularly at low WIMP masses (≤10 GeV) and by eliminating the need for recoil direction information when distinguishing canonical from non-canonical interactions.

title: From Cluster Core to Splashback: Linking Dynamical Structure to Multidimensional Galaxy Evolution in the Coma Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in the ApJ
summary: We investigate galaxy evolution across the full dynamical structure of the Coma cluster using the GalWCat19 spectroscopic cluster catalog combined with SDSS-based value-added galaxy properties. We measure a splashback radius of $R_{sp} = 2.94 \pm 0.16~h^{-1}\, Mpc$. Using specific star formation rate (sSFR), color offset from the red sequence ($Δ(g-r)_{RS}$), and bulge-to-total ratio ($B/T$) as independent diagnostics, we find a coherent environmental transition from quiescent, red, bulge-dominated galaxies in the cluster core to increasingly star-forming, blue, disk-dominated populations at larger radii. We further introduce a three-dimensional framework in the joint $(\log sSFR, Δ(g-r)_{RS}, B/T)$ space and develop a peak-based classification scheme that extends beyond traditional one-dimensional galaxy classifications. This framework identifies two dominant populations: red, quiescent, bulge-dominated galaxies, which account for $51\%$ of the joint-analysis sample, and blue, star-forming, disk-dominated galaxies, which account for $29\%$. The remaining $\sim20\%$ of galaxies occupy transitional or mixed states that connect these two principal populations. The relative fractions of these populations change strongly near the splashback radius, where the red, quiescent, bulge-dominated population declines rapidly and the blue, star-forming, disk-dominated population becomes increasingly dominant. These results show that the splashback boundary is not only a dynamical boundary, but also a critical evolutionary transition zone. Overall, our findings suggest that galaxy evolution in Coma is not a purely binary transformation, but instead proceeds through continuous multidimensional pathways in which star formation quenching, color evolution, and morphological transformation occur on different timescales while remaining closely linked to the cluster dynamical structure.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes galaxy evolution in the Coma cluster using the GalWCat19 catalog and SDSS data, measuring a splashback radius of 2.94±0.16 h⁻¹ Mpc. It introduces a three-dimensional classification framework (sSFR, color offset, bulge-to-total ratio) identifying red/quiescent/bulge-dominated (51%) and blue/star-forming/disk-dominated (29%) populations with ~20% in transitional states. The population fractions shift dramatically near the splashback radius, showing it acts as both a dynamical and evolutionary transition boundary. Galaxy evolution in Coma proceeds through continuous multidimensional pathways rather than binary transformations.
AI.motivation: To understand how galaxy properties such as star formation, color, and morphology are correlated with their host cluster's dynamical structure, and to determine whether environmental quenching is a binary process or a continuous multidimensional transformation that links to the splashback radius as a boundary.
AI.method: The authors combine the GalWCat19 spectroscopic cluster catalog with SDSS-based value-added galaxy properties for the Coma cluster. They measure the splashback radius and use three independent diagnostics—sSFR, color offset from the red sequence Δ(g−r)_RS, and B/T ratio—to characterize galaxy populations. They build a three-dimensional framework in joint (log sSFR, Δ(g−r)_RS, B/T) space with a peak-based classification scheme that extends beyond one-dimensional classification, then examine how population fractions vary with cluster-centric radius relative to the splashback boundary.
AI.result: The splashback radius is measured at 2.94±0.16 h⁻¹ Mpc. The joint three-dimensional framework identifies two dominant populations: red, quiescent, bulge-dominated galaxies (51% of the sample) and blue, star-forming, disk-dominated galaxies (29%), with ~20% in transitional/mixed states. The fraction of red, quiescent, bulge-dominated galaxies declines sharply near the splashback radius while blue, star-forming, disk-dominated galaxies become increasingly dominant there, indicating the splashback boundary is a critical evolutionary transition zone.
AI.conclusion: The splashback radius is not only a dynamical boundary but also a critical evolutionary transition zone. Galaxy evolution in the Coma cluster is not a purely binary transformation; it proceeds through continuous multidimensional pathways where quenching, color evolution, and morphological transformation occur on different timescales while remaining closely tied to the cluster's dynamical structure.

title: Evaporation of Primordial Black Holes with Multimodal Mass and Extended Spin Distributions: Cosmological Imprints on the Effective Number of Relativistic Species
summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs) form through several distinct mechanisms, each imprinting a characteristic mass function that a single-mass treatment risks erasing. Building on the FRISBHEE code, we introduce FRISHBEE, implementing four mass functions--log-normal, power-law, critical collapse, metric preheating--in a multimodal framework, with spin modeled via Gaussian and Fishbach profiles. Crucially, each channel's weight is derived from the primordial collapse probability rather than fitted, tying the mass function to the power-spectrum amplitude--a link between inflationary model-building and CMB observables. Solving the Friedmann-Boltzmann equations for $M_{\rm PBH}^{\rm in}=10^{7}$~g in the pre-BBN window, we compute $ΔN_{\rm eff}$ for five distributions, three spin configurations, and three weightings. Extended mass functions enhance $ΔN_{\rm eff}$ over the monochromatic benchmark by factors of $\sim\!1.03$ (critical collapse) to $\sim\!1.84$ (log-normal), preserving the hierarchy $LN > MM > PL > MP > CC$ across the mass window $\{10^{5},10^{7},10^{8}\}$~g. Near-extremal spin ($a_{\star}=0.99$) and spin-2 dark radiation invert this trend: superradiant spin loss averages away faster in broad distributions than in a monochromatic population, letting the monochromatic approximation overestimate $ΔN_{\rm eff}$. Against CMB-S4 and Simons Observatory sensitivities ($σ\simeq 0.06$ and $0.05$), the monochromatic benchmark is undetectable for scalar dark radiation (sDR $=0$), while log-normal, power-law, and multimodal distributions reach $\sim\!1.6$--$1.7σ$; for spin-2 dark radiation the signal drops over an order of magnitude, with none detectable. The formation channel thus governs the magnitude and observational accessibility of the Hawking signal, establishing $ΔN_{\rm eff}$ as a discriminant between single- and multi-channel PBH formation scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the FRISBHEE code into FRISHBEE to study primordial black hole (PBH) evaporation signatures, implementing four extended mass functions (log-normal, power-law, critical collapse, metric preheating) in a multimodal framework with physically-derived channel weights from primordial collapse probability. Computing ΔN_eff for a 10^7 g PBH in the pre-BBN window across various distributions, spins, and weightings, they find extended mass functions enhance ΔN_eff over monochromatic benchmarks by factors of 1.03–1.84, with near-extremal spin and spin-2 dark radiation inverting this trend. Against CMB-S4 and Simons Observatory sensitivities, only log-normal, power-law, and multimodal distributions reach ~1.6–1.7σ for scalar dark radiation, establishing ΔN_eff as a discriminant between single- and multi-channel PBH formation scenarios.
AI.motivation: Single-mass treatments of PBHs risk erasing the characteristic mass functions imprinted by distinct formation mechanisms. The authors aim to connect PBH formation channels to observational signatures (ΔN_eff) in a physically grounded way, avoiding ad hoc fitting of channel weights.
AI.method: Building on the FRISBHEE code, FRISHBEE implements four mass functions (log-normal, power-law, critical collapse, metric preheating) in a multimodal framework with spin modeled via Gaussian and Fishbach profiles. Channel weights are derived from primordial collapse probability, linking mass function to the power-spectrum amplitude. The Friedmann-Boltzmann equations are solved for M_PBH^in = 10^7 g in the pre-BBN window for five distributions, three spin configurations, and three weightings.
AI.result: Extended mass functions enhance ΔN_eff over the monochromatic benchmark by factors of ~1.03 (critical collapse) to ~1.84 (log-normal), preserving the hierarchy LN > MM > PL > MP > CC across the mass window {10^5, 10^7, 10^8} g. Near-extremal spin and spin-2 dark radiation invert this trend due to superradiant spin loss averaging. Against CMB-S4 and Simons Observatory sensitivities, monochromatic benchmarks are undetectable for scalar dark radiation while log-normal, power-law, and multimodal distributions reach ~1.6–1.7σ; for spin-2 dark radiation the signal drops by over an order of magnitude with none detectable.
AI.conclusion: The formation channel governs both the magnitude and observational accessibility of the Hawking signal from PBH evaporation. The extended mass function treatment establishes ΔN_eff as a discriminant between single- and multi-channel PBH formation scenarios, with detectability strongly dependent on whether the mass distribution is broad and on the spin/dark radiation configuration.

title: Does IRS13 require an intermediate-mass black hole?
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, to appear in Proceedings of IAU Symposium No. 405 "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time"
summary: We investigate whether the Galactic-centre association IRS13 requires an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) to remain bound. Using high-precision $N$-body calculations of IRS13-like systems orbiting the Milky Way supermassive black hole (SMBH), as well as simulations of more massive infalling clusters, we find that an IRS13-sized cluster dissolves on a very short timescale even when an IMBH of $4\times10^4\,M_\odot$ is present. The observed velocity dispersion can arise naturally from the tidal field of Sgr A* and the infall event itself; therefore, it need not imply a central IMBH. In the infalling-cluster runs, tidal stripping produces transient disks, spiral-like structures, and ring-like overdensities. These features suggest a broader interpretation: IRS13 is best viewed as a temporary phase-space overdensity, analogous in mechanism (though not in scale) to phase-wrapped shells and streams in disrupted galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether the Galactic-centre stellar association IRS13 requires an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) for its survival, using N-body simulations. IRS13-sized clusters dissolve quickly even with a 4×10^4 M⊙ IMBH present, and the observed velocity dispersion can be explained by the tidal field of Sgr A* and the infall event itself. IRS13 is better interpreted as a transient phase-space overdensity similar to tidal shells and streams in disrupted galaxies.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the existence and observed properties of the IRS13 stellar association in the Galactic centre necessarily imply the presence of an intermediate-mass black hole, or whether they can be explained by tidal interactions with the supermassive black hole Sgr A*.
AI.method: High-precision N-body simulations of IRS13-like systems orbiting the Milky Way supermassive black hole, including runs with an embedded IMBH of 4×10^4 M⊙, as well as simulations of more massive infalling clusters.
AI.result: IRS13-sized clusters dissolve on very short timescales even with an IMBH present. The observed velocity dispersion arises naturally from the Sgr A* tidal field and the infall event. Infalling-cluster simulations produce transient disks, spiral structures, and ring-like overdensities.
AI.conclusion: The observed properties of IRS13 need not imply a central IMBH. Instead, IRS13 is best understood as a temporary phase-space overdensity, analogous in mechanism (though not in scale) to phase-wrapped shells and streams in disrupted galaxies.

title: CORN -- Chronometers of Relic Nature I: The first estimate of the expansion rate of the Universe using compact relic galaxies
summary:
Measuring the expansion rate of the Universe is a central challenge in cosmology, particularly due to the persistent statistically significant discrepancy between the measurements of the Hubble constant, H0, obtained using early- and late-time probes, commonly known as the Hubble tension. Independent and robust methods are therefore essential to validate existing measurements and assess potential systematic effects.
  We employ the cosmic chronometer (CC) approach, which uses the differential age evolution of quiescent galaxies to measure the Hubble parameter H(z) without assuming an underlying cosmological model. In contrast to previous CC studies, we restrict our analysis to relics -- ultra compact massive galaxies (UCMGs) hosting the oldest stellar populations -- thereby minimising uncertainties related to star formation history and merger history.
  We employ the cosmic chronometer (CC) approach, which uses the differential age evolution of quiescent galaxies to measure the Hubble parameter H(z) without assuming an underlying cosmological model. In contrast to previous CC studies, we restrict our analysis to relics -- ultra compact massive galaxies (UCMGs) hosting the oldest stellar populations -- thereby minimising uncertainties related to star formation history and merger history.
  We obtain an independent measurement of H(z=0.15) = 85\pm53 km/s/Mpc.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the Hubble parameter using cosmic chronometers restricted to ultra-compact massive galaxies (relics) hosting the oldest stellar populations, obtaining an independent measurement of H(z=0.15) = 85 ± 53 km/s/Mpc, aimed at addressing the Hubble tension.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension—a statistically significant discrepancy between early- and late-time H0 measurements—requires independent and robust methods to validate existing measurements and assess potential systematic effects.
AI.method: The authors employ the cosmic chronometer approach, using the differential age evolution of quiescent galaxies to measure H(z) model-independently. Unlike previous CC studies, they restrict analysis to relics (UCMGs with the oldest stellar populations) to minimize uncertainties from star formation history and merger history.
AI.result: An independent measurement of H(z=0.15) = 85 ± 53 km/s/Mpc was obtained.
AI.conclusion: The relic-based cosmic chronometer approach provides an independent cosmological-model-free measurement of the expansion rate, contributing to the validation and cross-checking of existing H0 measurements in the context of the Hubble tension.

title: The Extended Mapping Obscuration to Reionization with ALMA (Ex-MORA) Survey: A Molecular Gas Line Search
summary:
Current investigations of cold gas in the interstellar medium face selection biases, as optical/near-infrared surveys favor massive, low-obscuration galaxies and miss gas-rich passive or inefficient star-forming systems. Overcoming this requires large-volume line surveys selected by molecular gas rather than stellar luminosity. We present a molecular gas census across $0.5 < z < 5$ using ALMA Band 4 observations from the Extended Mapping of Obscuration to Reionization Survey (Ex-MORA), covering 577 arcmin$^2$. Combining an unbiased search for bright emitters with a targeted search using spectroscopic redshift priors, we detect 52 galaxies in CO or \ci transitions (two showing two lines). Physical properties were derived via \texttt{CIGALE} with non-parametric star-formation histories, and gas masses were estimated using metallicity-dependent conversion factors.
  The sample is dominated by main-sequence (MS) galaxies with high stellar masses (median $\log M_*/\text{M}_{\odot} = 10.83$) and large gas reservoirs ($>10^{10}\,\text{M}_{\odot}$). Gas fraction ($μ_{\text{gas}}$) increases with redshift for active populations, though high-redshift trends are influenced by a gas-rich protocluster at $z \approx 2.4$. Conversely, an overdensity at $z \approx 0.73$ mirrors the field population. Five Green Valley (GV) galaxies exhibit a $μ_{\text{gas}}$ peak at cosmic noon, suggesting stellar feedback may suppress star formation by heating gas rather than rapidly depleting it in at least some transitional systems. Resolved kinematics show a prevalence of rotating disks. These results demonstrate that wide-area line searches effectively recover massive gas reservoirs across diverse evolutionary stages

AI.tldr: The Ex-MORA survey uses ALMA Band 4 to perform a molecular gas census across 0.5 < z < 5 over 577 arcmin², detecting 52 galaxies in CO or CI lines. The sample is dominated by massive main-sequence galaxies with large gas reservoirs; gas fractions increase with redshift (influenced by a gas-rich protocluster at z≈2.4), while Green Valley galaxies show a gas fraction peak at cosmic noon, suggesting stellar feedback suppresses star formation by heating gas rather than depleting it quickly.
AI.motivation: Current cold gas studies are biased by optical/near-infrared selection that favors massive, low-obscuration galaxies and misses gas-rich passive or inefficient star-forming systems. Large-volume line surveys selected by molecular gas rather than stellar luminosity are needed to overcome these biases.
AI.method: The survey combines an unbiased search for bright emitters with a targeted search using spectroscopic redshift priors in ALMA Band 4 data from Ex-MORA (577 arcmin²). Physical properties were derived using CIGALE with non-parametric star-formation histories, and gas masses were estimated using metallicity-dependent CO-to-H2 conversion factors.
AI.result: 52 galaxies detected in CO or CI (two with two lines), dominated by main-sequence galaxies with high stellar masses (median log M*/M⊙ = 10.83) and large gas reservoirs (>10^10 M⊙). Gas fraction increases with redshift for active populations, though high-redshift trends are affected by a gas-rich protocluster at z≈2.4; an overdensity at z≈0.73 mirrors the field. Five Green Valley galaxies show a gas fraction peak at cosmic noon. Resolved kinematics show prevalence of rotating disks.
AI.conclusion: Wide-area molecular gas line searches effectively recover massive gas reservoirs across diverse evolutionary stages, and the Green Valley gas peak suggests stellar feedback may suppress star formation by heating gas rather than rapidly depleting it in at least some transitional systems.

title: Evidence for Enhancement in the Rate of Fast Radio Bursts Toward Galaxy Clusters
comment: 31 Pages (8 Appendix) 17 Figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Massive galaxy clusters can introduce gravitational lensing and populations of suppressed star formation member galaxies into the line of sight, potentially changing the distribution of observable sources toward them from that of the average sky. As a result, Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) aligned with galaxy clusters can provide a unique window into parameter spaces of the FRB population that other lines of sight do not afford. In this study, we demonstrate that the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog contains FRBs emitted from within or behind clusters identified from the latest DECaLS data release; we isolate a sample of 26 FRBs where this is likely, including one repeating FRB and two FRBs that intersect the Coma cluster. Comparing our results against a range of simulated FRB populations, we conclude that the number of these associations represents a $3σ$ rate enhancement toward galaxy clusters, constituting $1.4\pm0.4\%$ of the FRBs detected in the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog. We suggest that this enhancement is caused by an equal proportion of member galaxies hosting additional FRBs, and gravitational lensing magnifying background sources. We demonstrate that such contributions are sensitive to alternative progenitor channels and high redshift evolution in the FRB population, providing a future avenue for constraining these features. Considering the redshifts and masses of the associated clusters, we identify FRB 20211113A, which is aligned with the strong gravitational lens Abell 2218 as a potential lensed candidate for further consideration.

AI.tldr: FRBs aligned with massive galaxy clusters show a 3σ rate enhancement (1.4±0.4% of the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog), attributed equally to member galaxies hosting additional FRBs and gravitational lensing magnification. 26 FRBs are identified as likely cluster-associated, including one repeater and two intersecting the Coma cluster. FRB 20211113A, aligned with Abell 2218, is flagged as a potential lensed candidate.
AI.motivation: Galaxy clusters in the foreground can gravitationally lens and host suppressed star formation galaxies, altering the observable FRB distribution along those lines of sight. This provides a unique window into FRB population parameter spaces (progenitor channels, high-redshift evolution) that other sightlines cannot probe.
AI.method: Using the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog and the latest DECaLS cluster data, the authors identify FRBs whose lines of sight pass through foreground clusters. They isolate 26 likely associations and compare against simulated FRB populations to quantify the statistical significance and enhancement rates.
AI.result: 26 FRBs are likely aligned with clusters, including one repeating FRB and two intersecting the Coma cluster. The measured enhancement is a 3σ rate enhancement, comprising 1.4±0.4% of the catalog. The enhancement is split equally between member-galaxy FRBs and lensed background sources.
AI.conclusion: Cluster-aligned FRB enhancements are sensitive to alternative progenitor channels and high-redshift evolution, offering a new avenue to constrain these FRB population features. FRB 20211113A behind Abell 2218 is identified as a promising lensed candidate for further study.

title: Constructing X-ray Spectral Models of Galaxies: Varying Contributions from X-ray Binary Populations with Host Galaxy Properties
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal (ApJ). 19 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables
summary: Recent work has shown that the emission from X-ray binary (XRB) populations in galaxies varies with stellar mass ($M_\star$), star formation rate (SFR), and metallicity ($Z$). Such scaling relations are widely used to predict the XRB contributions to galaxy-integrated X-ray luminosities including studies focused on dwarf active galactic nuclei (AGN) and the X-ray radiation field during the epoch of heating in the early ($z \geq 8$) universe. However, as galaxies approach low SFR and low $Z$, the relatively shallow slope of the XRB luminosity function (XLF) can yield very large stochastic variations in the total X-ray luminosity expected from the XRB population, for fixed values of $M_\star$, SFR, and $Z$. We have created a procedure to statistically sample any XLF and model total X-ray spectra for XRB populations and their stochastic uncertainties. We demonstrate the accuracy of this procedure using data for galaxies ranging from high to low $M_\star$, SFR, and $Z$ and generating X-ray spectral models consistent with Chandra observations. For galaxies that lie on the galactic main-sequence, we can relate SFR and $Z$ to $M_\star$ using established $M_\star$-SFR and $M_\star$-$Z$ relations. Applying these relations, we construct main-sequence (MS) XRB spectral models, which provide typical XRB spectral shapes, normalizations, and uncertainties as a function of $M_\star$. The spectral model library associated with this work is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20126734.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a statistical procedure for sampling X-ray binary (XRB) luminosity functions and generating stochastic X-ray spectral models for XRB populations. It accounts for the large stochastic variations in galaxy-integrated X-ray luminosity that arise at low SFR and low metallicity. The method is validated against Chandra observations and applied to main-sequence galaxies to construct a spectral model library as a function of stellar mass.
AI.motivation: XRB emission scaling relations with stellar mass, SFR, and metallicity are widely used to predict galaxy-integrated X-ray luminosities (e.g., for dwarf AGN studies and the epoch of heating at z≥8). However, at low SFR and low Z, the shallow XLF slope produces very large stochastic variations in total expected XRB luminosity for fixed galaxy properties, requiring a framework that properly handles these uncertainties.
AI.method: The authors develop a statistical sampling procedure for any XRB luminosity function that generates total X-ray spectral models for XRB populations along with their stochastic uncertainties. They validate the procedure against data from galaxies spanning a wide range of stellar mass, SFR, and Z, generating spectral models consistent with Chandra observations. They then link SFR and Z to stellar mass via established M*-SFR and M*-Z relations to construct main-sequence XRB spectral models as a function of stellar mass.
AI.result: The procedure accurately reproduces XRB X-ray spectral models consistent with Chandra observations across galaxies from high to low stellar mass, SFR, and metallicity. The resulting main-sequence XRB spectral models provide typical spectral shapes, normalizations, and uncertainties as a function of stellar mass. A public spectral model library is released.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a robust framework for modeling stochastic XRB emission and its uncertainties, particularly important in regimes (low SFR, low Z) where standard scaling relations break down due to XLF sampling effects. The associated spectral model library enables more reliable predictions of XRB contributions to galaxy X-ray emission, relevant for dwarf AGN searches and high-redshift reionization-era studies.

title: Evolution of Neutron Star Environment in the Galactic Halo : Implications for Dark Matter Accretion
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, Prepared for submission to JCAP
summary: Neutron stars (NS) are one of the indirect detection probes for dark matter (DM). The presence of DM is known to affect the observable properties of NS. Theoretical calculations for various equations of state of a DM admixed NS lead to estimates of the DM mass in a NS of the order of $10^{-2} M_{\odot}$. On the other hand, simplistic estimates of the amount of DM that is accreted on to the NS in the Solar neighborhood, over its age, suggest that this number is of the order $10^{-14} M_{\odot}$. Various studies have addressed this non-agreement theoretically by explaining the mechanisms leading to higher fraction than expected from smooth spherically symmetric accretion. In this work, we attempt to assess the role of the dynamic DM environmental density in the Galactic halo to explain possible enhancement in DM accretion. We consider a high resolution N-body simulation and method of Voronoi tessellation to calculate local DM density around putative NS locations in a statistically representative sample of Milky Way analogues. We infer that the dynamics of substructure may enhance the DM mass in NS by about a factor 2 as compared to the baseline, spherically symmetric expectation. Environmental effects therefore cannot explain the orders of magnitude discrepancy between equation of state and accretion based estimates of DM admixed in NS.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether dynamic dark matter (DM) environmental density in the Galactic halo can explain the discrepancy between theoretical DM mass estimates in neutron stars (from equations of state, ~10^-2 M_sun) and simplistic accretion-based estimates (~10^-14 M_sun). Using high-resolution N-body simulations and Voronoi tessellation to compute local DM densities around neutron stars in Milky Way analogues, they find substructure dynamics enhance DM accretion by only a factor of ~2 over the baseline. This is insufficient to reconcile the several orders of magnitude discrepancy between the two estimates.
AI.motivation: There is a significant discrepancy between theoretical estimates of DM mass in neutron stars derived from equations of state (~10^-2 M_sun) and simplistic estimates from smooth spherically symmetric DM accretion (~10^-14 M_sun). The authors aim to determine whether dynamic DM environmental density in the Galactic halo, particularly substructure, can explain this enhancement in the accreted DM mass.
AI.method: The authors employ a high-resolution N-body simulation to model the Galactic halo and use the Voronoi tessellation method to calculate local DM density around putative neutron star locations. They consider a statistically representative sample of Milky Way analogues and compare the DM accretion with substructure dynamics against the baseline spherically symmetric accretion scenario.
AI.result: The dynamics of DM substructure can enhance the DM mass in neutron stars by approximately a factor of 2 compared to the baseline spherically symmetric expectation. This enhancement is far too small to account for the orders of magnitude discrepancy between equation-of-state-based and accretion-based DM estimates in neutron stars.
AI.conclusion: Environmental effects from Galactic halo substructure cannot explain the large discrepancy between equation-of-state-based and accretion-based estimates of DM mass admixed in neutron stars. This suggests that other mechanisms or considerations are needed to reconcile the theoretical predictions.

title: The Rotation Curve of the Milky Way: State of the Art, the Keplerian Decline Debate, and Implications for Dark Matter
comment: 40 pages, 12 figures
summary: For four decades, the roughly flat rotation curve (RC) of the Milky Way (MW) stood as local evidence for an extended dark matter (DM) halo. \textit{Gaia} DR3 has changed the picture: several analyses now find a velocity decline beyond R \approx 15\kpc, and the most radical interpretation \citep{jiao2023} claims a nearly Keplerian fall-off (\vc \propto R^{-1/2}) that excludes a flat RC at 3σand implies a total dynamical mass of only \sim 2 \times 10^{11}\Msun---three to five times below pre-\textit{Gaia} estimates. Taken at face value, this would make the MW exceptional among comparable spirals and challenge both \LambdaCDM and MOND. It would also alter predictions for direct-detection experiments, although the local DM density is not fixed by virial mass alone. The Keplerian claim rests on the delicate assumptions of axisymmetric Jeans modelling, while stellar streams, globular clusters, satellite kinematics, and the Local Group timing argument generally favour a substantially heavier halo, and cosmological simulations reveal potentially substantial biases in Jeans-inferred outer RCs. This review offers a self-contained, pedagogical account of the debate: we derive the full formalism from first principles---the Jeans equations, the asymmetric drift correction, the standard DM halo and baryonic mass models, the MOND flat-RC prediction, and the timing argument---present an illustrative phenomenological MCMC fit and a Gaussian Process reconstruction of the RC, and critically assess which features of the decline can be regarded as established and which remain open.

AI.tldr: A pedagogical review of the Milky Way rotation curve debate, examining claims of a Keplerian (rather than flat) fall-off beyond ~15 kpc from Gaia DR3 data, and critically assessing whether this decline is established or an artifact of Jeans modeling assumptions.
AI.motivation: Gaia DR3 observations have led to claims of a declining (near-Keplerian) Milky Way rotation curve beyond ~15 kpc, contradicting the long-standing flat rotation curve that motivated dark matter. Taken at face value this would challenge both ΛCDM and MOND, make the MW exceptional among spirals, and alter dark matter detection predictions. The debate has major cosmological and experimental implications, warranting a careful review.
AI.method: The paper derives the full rotation curve formalism from first principles (Jeans equations, asymmetric drift correction, standard DM halo and baryonic mass models, MOND flat-RC prediction, timing argument), presents an illustrative phenomenological MCMC fit and a Gaussian Process reconstruction of the RC, and critically compares the Keplerian claim against evidence from stellar streams, globular clusters, satellite kinematics, the Local Group timing argument, and cosmological simulations of Jeans-inference biases.
AI.result: The review finds the Keplerian fall-off claim is fragile, resting on delicate axisymmetric Jeans modelling assumptions. Independent tracers (stellar streams, globular clusters, satellites, timing argument) favor a substantially heavier halo, and cosmological simulations indicate potentially large biases in Jeans-inferred outer rotation curves. The analysis demarcates which features of the decline are robustly established versus which remain open questions.
AI.conclusion: The claimed Keplerian decline of the Milky Way rotation curve is not on solid footing; the apparent velocity drop is likely at least partly attributable to systematic biases in the Jeans modeling approach. A heavy dark matter halo remains favored by multiple independent probes, though a mildly declining outer rotation curve cannot be fully excluded.

title: Fitting trends in quasar emission and absorption line redshifts
summary:
The spectrum of a quasar consists of a few emission lines whose wavelengths are shifted by similar redshifts and numerous absorption lines whose wavelengths are shifted by different redshifts. Hence each quasar is characterised by an emission line redshift and the absorption lines redshifts are all less than the emission line redshift. The distribution of observed absorption line redshifts ($z_{abs}$) with respect to emission line redshift ($z_{em}$) for a large sample of quasars shows a systematic trend as pointed out by \citet{2016arXiv160901593K}. They noticed that increase in $z_{em}$ is accompanied by a monotonic increase in the lowest detected value of $z_{abs}$ and inferred that the emission and absorption lines were all formed in the quasar.
  This study focuses on modeling the systematic trend in the observed $z_{em} \rightarrow z_{abs}$ distribution. We considered the redshift data of absorption lines of singly ionized magnesium (denoted by MgII) and triply ionized carbon (denoted by CIV) for a large sample of quasars. We find that the envelope of data points defining the lowest value of the MgII absorption line redshift (which we denote by $z_{MgIImodel}$) for a given $z_{em}$ satisfies $z_{MgIImodel} = (0.418 \pm 0.008) z_{em} - (0.482 \pm 0.02)$ with an $R^2$ value of 0.99. The model can be used to predict the lowest expected MgII absorption line redshift for any $z_{em}$. We find a similar model for the lowest expected redshift of triply ionized carbon lines for any $z_{em}$ which is $z_{CIVmodel} = 0.845 (\pm 0.0002) z_{em} - 0.153 (\pm 0.0006)$.

AI.tldr: This study models the systematic trend in quasar emission vs. absorption line redshifts, deriving linear relationships for the lowest detected MgII and CIV absorption line redshifts as functions of the emission line redshift.
AI.motivation: To model the previously observed systematic trend in the zem → zabs distribution for quasars and provide predictive relationships for the lowest expected absorption line redshifts.
AI.method: Analysis of redshift data for MgII and CIV absorption lines from a large sample of quasars, fitting the envelope of data points defining the lowest absorption line redshift as a function of emission line redshift using linear regression.
AI.result: Two linear models were derived: zMgIImodel = (0.418 ± 0.008) z_em - (0.482 ± 0.02) with R² = 0.99 for MgII, and zCIVmodel = 0.845 (± 0.0002) z_em - 0.153 (± 0.0006) for CIV.
AI.conclusion: The models can predict the lowest expected MgII and CIV absorption line redshifts for any given emission line redshift, providing a quantitative framework for understanding quasar emission-absorption line relationships.

title: Electron temperature and emission measure of HII regions in the central molecular zone (CMZ) from H40 αrecombination line and continuum emissions by ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey - ACES -
comment: 20 pages, 17 pages, 2 tables, accepted for PASJ 08.08.2026
summary: Star formation activity in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) directly manifests itself as radio continuum free-free emission (Bremsstrahlung) and radio recombination line emission from HII regions surrounding newly formed massive stars. We derive the overall distribution of the HII regions and their fundamental properties: electron temperature ($\Te$) and emission measure ($EM$), and hence electron density in the form of two dimensional distribution maps over the CMZ by analyzing the ACES (ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey) \h40 (99.02 GHz) recombination line and 99.6 GHz continuum emission data with synthesized beam widths of $2''.45$ (0.097 pc at 8.2 kpc) and $2''.14$, respectively. We apply the 'TeEM' method ($\Te$--$EM$ mapping), which creates $\Te$ and $EM$ maps from input 2D maps of the continuum and integrated line intensity. The analysis covers the entire ACES field from $l\sim -0^\circ.6$ to $+0^\circ.8$ and from $b\sim -0^\circ.2$ to $+0^\circ.1$. The area analyzed is complete and includes previously known HII regions such as Sgr B2, Sgr B1, the Sickle, the Pistol, thermal filaments (Bridges), Sgr A HII regions, the Minispiral, and many other known HII regions. Sgr C is not included in the analysis due to the insufficient signal-to-noise ratio in the recombination line map. The mean electron temperature over the CMZ is determined to be $\Tcmz= 5872 \pm 78 ~{\rm (SE)} ~\pm 3682~{\rm (SD)}$ K (SE:standard error of the mean, SD: pixel-to-pixel standard deviation). Some HII regions, such as Sgr B2 Main and the Minispiral, exhibit large scatter and an internal $\Te$ gradient of several thousand K per parsec. title: Fine-tuning in mixed Dark Matter models with Primordial Black Hole relics
comment: 20 pages + appendix, 5 figures
summary: We investigate the fine-tuning of a tripartite dark matter (DM) scenario involving ultra-light primordial black holes (PBHs), whose evaporation before Big Bang Nucleosynthesis leaves Planck-mass relics and produces DM particles together with an independently produced DM component. We uniformly evaluate the parameter sensitivity required to reproduce the observed DM abundance, $Ω_{\rm DM}$. Considering thermal WIMP freeze-out, freeze-in, and QCD axion misalignment, and assuming PBHs form via collapse of perturbations following horizon entry, we find that the fine-tuning is normally dominated by the structure of the PBH relic abundance calculation rather than by the particle DM candidate or the details of PBH evaporation. In radiation-dominated cosmologies, the DM abundance is highly sensitive to the primordial curvature power spectrum because the PBH formation fraction depends exponentially on density fluctuations. Although an early PBH-dominated era dilutes pre-existing abundances and reduces the apparent tuning of the PBH abundance, inflationary fine-tuning remains required to produce the required initial large amplitude perturbations. We further examine alternative PBH formation channels, including supercooled first-order phase transitions and collapsing domain walls, and find that they replace the inflationary fine-tuning with alternative exponential sensitivities. We conclude that a natural realization of an order unity PBH relic abundance is hard to motivate.

The authors find that fine-tuning is dominated by the exponential sensitivity of PBH formation to density fluctuations in the primordial curvature power spectrum, rather than by the particle DM candidate or evaporation details. Alternative PBH formation channels (supercooled phase transitions, collapsing domain walls) replace inflationary fine-tuning with other exponential sensitivities, leading to the conclusion that a natural order-unity PBH relic abundance is hard to motivate.

title: Scaling Relations of Galactic Outflows Across Cosmic Time: New Insights from Cosmic Noon
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 3 + 2 tables, accepted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Galactic outflows play a significant role in regulating galaxy evolution. Scaling relations between stellar mass ($M_\ast$), star formation (SFR), and outflow properties have been extensively studied at low redshifts ($z<1$) but less so beyond $z \sim 2$. We construct a joint sample of 387 galaxies from $z \sim$ 0-9, including 98 new Cosmic Noon galaxies from the Keck Baryonic Structure Survey and the Keck Lyman Continuum Spectroscopic Survey. Using high signal-to-noise emission lines (SNR $>$ 50 for H$α$ or [OIII] $\lambda5007$) from Keck/MOSFIRE spectra, we detect warm-ionized outflows by decomposing lines into narrow and broad components. With the joint sample, we explore the redshift evolution of outflow scaling relations. On average, outflows at Cosmic Noon have higher maximum velocities than those at low$-z$ by up to a factor of 3 for a fixed $M_\ast$, SFR, or SFR surface density. They also have higher mass outflow rates for a fixed $M_\ast$. Despite faster and stronger outflows, there is no evolution in the mass loading factor for a fixed $M_\ast$. We find evidence for galactic fountains, as the majority of outflowing gas is recycled at a radius of $\sim$0.03 R$_\textrm{vir}$. We also constrain the overall outflow occurrence rate in our galaxy sample to be at least 30$\%$ when taking galaxy orientation and outflow geometry into account. By analyzing the largest sample of warm-ionized outflows at Cosmic Noon to date and compiling large galaxy samples across all redshifts, we present a comprehensive analysis of galactic outflows throughout cosmic time.

title: Beyond Feedback: Disentangling Baryonic Effects with tSZ$\times$FRB Cross-Correlations
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Standard observational probes lack the sensitivity to characterize the interplay between feedback-driven gas ejection and non-thermal pressure support in groups and clusters, and current models lack the framework to disentangle it. Recent first detections of the tSZ$\times$FRB cross-power spectrum (Takahashi et al, 2025; Sharma et al 2026) have been interpreted as constraining AGN feedback and $σ_8$, but the baryon models used do not independently parameterize non-thermal pressure support, leaving feedback efficiency and gas thermodynamics degenerate. We demonstrate that this cross-correlation provides sensitivity to the thermal and non-thermal structure of cluster gas that neither observable alone can achieve, because the tSZ effect traces electron pressure while FRBs trace solely electron density. Using the Baryon Pasting (BP) framework, which separately parameterizes feedback efficiency $ε_f$ and non-thermal pressure amplitude $A_{\rm nt}$, we show that their joint constraint breaks this degeneracy. In the noise-free limit, adding the cross-power spectrum reduces $r_{\rm cond}$ from $0.96$ to $0.08$ (a 12-fold reduction) and improves the joint figure of merit by a factor of 19, with the constraining power concentrated at cluster interior scales ($\ell \gtrsim 3000$). Recent detections are consistent with our fiducial model and disfavor weak feedback ($ε_f^{95\%} \gtrsim 2.40\text{--}3.67 \times 10^{-6}$ across datasets). With $5\times10^4$ FRBs from DSA-2000 combined with SO, we forecast $3.8\%$ fractional precision on $A_{\rm nt}$, improving to $2.3\%$ with CMB-HD. These constraints directly inform the hydrostatic mass bias, with immediate implications for cluster-based cosmological inference from eROSITA, SO, and CMB-HD.

title: Estimating the local star formation rate density from ASKAP RACS
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, published in PASA
summary: Understanding the evolution of the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) is key to uncovering how the Universe arrived at its present state. This paper presents a novel and efficient method to estimate the local SFRD, which uses supervised machine learning to first identify a population of star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Next, star-formation rates (SFRs) are determined using the 1.4-GHz radio-continuum emission detected by the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). Specifically, a gradient-boosted decision tree model was implemented to classify extragalactic sources from the Beck et al. (2022, MNRAS, 515, 4711) catalogue as either galaxies or quasars using RACS-mid and WISE photometry. The full sample, consisting of 389,392 sources, was partitioned into a 70%-15%-15% split for training, validating, and testing. The optimised model achieved a weighted F1 score of 0.93 and an accuracy of 0.94 on the test dataset, ultimately classifying 336,674 sources as galaxies and 52,718 sources as quasars. Using the resulting $z<0.1$ depth-matched galaxy sample and the photometric redshift predictions from Beck et al. (2022, MNRAS, 515, 4711), a modified 1.4-GHz SFR calibration was determined, yielding a local, completeness-corrected, $z<0.1$ SFRD of $(1.4 \pm 0.5) \times 10^{-2} \; \rm M_{\odot}\, yr^{-1}\,Mpc^{-3}$ using 11,293 sources. This value is consistent with previous results. Thus, this study demonstrates the feasibility of using supervised learning to identify large populations of SFGs in order to investigate the SFRD evolution. This presents an exciting prospect for future, deeper surveys such as EMU, which will enable the cosmic SFRD to be probed out to higher redshifts.
