title: Mapping the Inner Milky Way with Infrared-Derived Distances to AGB Stars
comment: 22 pages, 16 figures and 5 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The structure and evolution of the Milky Way (MW) can be traced with distance estimates to the evolved stellar populations in the inner galactic region. However, direct astrometric distances remain unavailable or highly uncertain for the majority of these sources due to instrumental limitations, large angular diameters, and complex variability. In this work, we develop a supervised machine-learning model to estimate statistical distances to oxygen-rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars selected from the AKARI mid-infrared survey. We build an XGBoost regression model that maps multi-band IR photometry to distance using a training set of AGB stars with previously derived SED-based distances achieving a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 6% on an independent test set. Distance estimates for over 36,000 AGB sources are obtained within a 36% total error margin, greatly expanding distance coverage (0.5-20 kpc) for dust-obscured AGB populations in the Galactic plane. We find good agreement with reported distances for Galactic Mira variables and independent period-luminosity relations. Utilizing the expanded distance set, we further investigate the spatial distribution of Mira variables in the Galactic bulge and disk. Longer-period Miras preferentially trace the bulge's barred morphology compared to their shorter-period counterparts that populate the disk. We also find roughly constant, but differing, relative scale heights for the bulge and disk, with the bulge vertical dispersion about 30% larger. These findings show that IR photometry-derived statistical distances can recover large-scale Galactic structures and establish long-period Mira variables as efficient tracers of stellar populations in heavily obscured regions of the MW.

The expanded distance catalog (0.5-20 kpc) is used to trace Galactic structure, revealing that long-period Miras trace the bulge's barred morphology while shorter-period Miras populate the disk, and showing the bulge has ~30% larger vertical dispersion than the disk.
AI.motivation: Direct astrometric distances to evolved stellar populations in the inner Milky Way are unavailable or highly uncertain due to instrumental limitations, large angular diameters, and complex variability, hindering studies of the Galaxy's structure and evolution.
AI.method: A supervised XGBoost regression model maps multi-band IR photometry from the AKARI mid-infrared survey to distance, trained on AGB stars with previously derived SED-based distances.

AI.conclusion: IR photometry-derived statistical distances can recover large-scale Galactic structures, and long-period Mira variables serve as efficient tracers of stellar populations in heavily obscured regions of the Milky Way.

title: A Wandering 35,000-Solar-Mass Black Hole Fed by a Gravitational Wake
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Submitted
summary: Intermediate-mass black holes are widely considered to be the seeds of supermassive black holes, a substantial population of which is expected to remain displaced from galactic nuclei owing to hierarchical galaxy assembly and inefficient dynamical friction. While several fueling channels can sustain central black holes, those pathways are largely inaccessible to off-nuclear black holes, leaving their fuel supply uncertain. As these wandering black holes move through the interstellar medium of their host galaxies, theory predicts that they can capture gas from the dense wake produced by gravitational focusing. However, direct observational evidence for this process has remained elusive. Here we report evidence for a wandering intermediate-mass black hole of 35,000 solar mass accreting through such a gravitational wake. Its black-hole nature is supported by broad-line emission, a compact continuum counterpart, long-term optical variability, and a power-law-like spectral energy distribution. Multi-epoch spectroscopy reveals three distinct gas components: a blueshifted, low-density upstream flow; a redshifted, dense downstream wake; and optically thick absorbers well within the capture radius that drive rapid changing-look variability in the broad-line emission. This discovery establishes a previously unobserved channel for the growth of wandering intermediate-mass black holes.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first observational evidence of a wandering intermediate-mass black hole (~35,000 solar masses) accreting gas from the dense gravitational wake it creates as it moves through its host galaxy's interstellar medium, establishing a new fueling channel for off-nuclear black holes.

While fueling channels exist for central black holes, off-nuclear or "wandering" black holes lack access to these pathways, leaving their gas supply mechanism uncertain. Theory predicts they can capture gas from the wake produced by gravitational focusing, but direct observational evidence had been elusive.

They used multi-epoch spectroscopy to characterize three distinct gas components: a blueshifted low-density upstream flow, a redshifted dense downstream wake, and optically thick absorbers within the capture radius driving rapid changing-look variability in the broad-line emission.

title: SIRIUS Project: Dynamical Evolution of Primordial Binaries during Star Cluster Formation
comment: 11 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Binary populations are closely linked to the star formation process; however, their primordial properties can be changed by subsequent dynamical interactions within their natal clusters. The aim of this study is to clarify how different primordial binary populations affect the evolution of multiplicity and the global structure of forming star clusters. We investigate the dynamical evolution of primordial binaries during star cluster formation using self-consistent Nbody/smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations that follow the collapse of a molecular cloud to a star cluster. We systematically compare three star formation models: close binary (CB), wide binary (WB), and single star (SS) formation model. In CB and WB models, the multiplicity fraction decreases with time due to dynamical interactions. In particular, the fraction in the WB model drops to a level comparable to that in the SS model. The multiplicity fraction of high-mass stars is similarly high in all models, whereas only the CB model shows a relatively high fraction for low-mass stars. Due to the assumption of equal-mass binary formation, the CB and WB models exhibit an excess at q= 1 in the mass-ratio distribution, while the SS model has no clear trend. Frequent few-body interactions generate distinct stellar populations inside and outside the cluster: the multiplicity fraction within the cluster is systematically higher, while mass functions in the outside have a shallower slope. Finally, stellar density profiles in the clusters are broadly similar among all models. The primordial binary population significantly affects the final binary properties, while having only a limited impact on their host cluster structures. Our results suggest that close binaries need to form at the star formation stage to reproduce the observed multiplicity fraction of low-mass stars and the excess of equal-mass binaries.

Results show that primordial binaries strongly affect final binary properties—close binaries are needed to reproduce observed multiplicity of low-mass stars—but have limited impact on host cluster structures like density profiles.
AI.motivation: Binary populations are linked to star formation, but their primordial properties can be modified by dynamical interactions in natal clusters. The authors aim to clarify how different primordial binary populations affect the multiplicity evolution and global structure of forming clusters to better understand the origin of observed binary properties.
AI.method: Self-consistent Nbody/smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations track the collapse of a molecular cloud into a star cluster. Three star formation models are systematically compared: close binary (CB), wide binary (WB), and single star (SS) formation, with equal-mass binary formation assumed.
AI.result: Multiplicity fraction decreases over time due to dynamical interactions, especially in the WB model which drops to levels comparable to the SS model. High-mass stars show similarly high multiplicity fractions in all models, while only CB shows relatively high fractions for low-mass stars. CB and WB models exhibit an excess at q=1 in mass-ratio distributions. Few-body interactions create distinct populations: higher multiplicity inside clusters and shallower mass function slopes outside. Stellar density profiles are broadly similar across all models.
AI.conclusion: Primordial binaries significantly influence final binary properties but have limited impact on host cluster structures. Close binaries must form at the star formation stage to reproduce the observed multiplicity fraction of low-mass stars and the equal-mass binary excess.

title: ATLAS. III. Dust Around Little Red Dots: Hydrogen Line Ratios beyond Dust-free Non-Case B Models
comment: 26 pages, 10 figures in the main text, 8 figures in the Appendix, 2 Tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome
summary: We investigate broad hydrogen line ratios in little red dots (LRDs) using five high-redshift ($z>2$) sources from JWST/NIRSpec medium/high-resolution spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive and fifteen low-redshift sources ($z=0.1$--$0.9$) from the literature, all with broad H$β$ detected at $>5σ$. After carefully measuring the broad-line fluxes while accounting for absorption features and neighboring emission lines, we find that the broad H$α$/H$β$ ratios are very high, ranging from 6 to 30, well above the Case B recombination value. Using plane-parallel \textsc{Cloudy} photoionization models with the total line emission from both sides of the slab, we investigate the physical origin of the broad hydrogen line ratios beyond Case B, jointly modeling the Balmer and Paschen line ratios for the subset of one high-$z$ and two low-$z$ LRDs with detected broad Paschen lines. We find that one low-$z$ LRD is reproduced by a high gas number density ($\log (n_{\mathrm H}/{\rm cm^{-3}})\sim10$--11) on the broad-line H$α$/H$β$--Pa$β$/Pa$γ$ plane, whereas the remaining two LRDs additionally require substantial dust extinction of $E(B-V)\gtrsim0.2$--$1.0$, even after accounting for non-Case B effects. Since the narrow H$α$/H$β$ ratios do not indicate such large dust extinction, these results demonstrate that the obscuring dust is spatially associated with the broad-line region. Even without Paschen-line measurements, two and eight LRDs in the high- and low-redshift samples, respectively, exhibit H$α$/H$β>13$, which cannot be reproduced by the non-Case B models, suggesting that dust obscuration might be common among LRDs, occurring in at least about half of the population. Such dust may represent a lower-column-density counterpart of the dusty torus in AGNs, reconciling the weak hot-dust emission.

Using Cloudy photoionization modeling, they show these ratios require either extremely high gas densities or substantial dust extinction within the broad-line region itself, suggesting that dust obscuration is common in LRDs and represents a lower-column-density counterpart to AGN dusty tori.
AI.motivation: Little red dots (LRDs) are a newly discovered class of high-redshift compact objects whose nature remains uncertain—whether they host AGNs or are dominated by stellar processes. Broad hydrogen line ratios that exceed Case B recombination values can reveal the physical conditions (density, dust) in their broad-line regions, helping to understand the powering mechanism and geometry of these objects.

They carefully separate broad Hα, Hβ, and Paschen lines while accounting for absorption and neighboring emission. They use plane-parallel Cloudy photoionization models (including both sides of the slab emission) to jointly model Balmer and Paschen line ratios, fitting on the Hα/Hβ vs Paβ/Paγ plane to disentangle density and extinction effects.

One low-z LRD is explained solely by high gas density (log n_H/cm^-3 ~ 10-11), while two other LRDs require additional dust extinction of E(B-V) ~ 0.2-1.0 even after accounting for non-Case B effects. Since narrow-line ratios do not show such large extinction, the dust is spatially associated with the broad-line region. Additionally, 2 high-z and 8 low-z LRDs with Hα/Hβ > 13 cannot be explained by non-Case B models alone, implying dust obscuration occurs in at least ~50% of the LRD population.

title: The Radcliffe Wave is not alone in the Local System
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to astronomy Letters
summary: The spatial distribution of open star clusters (OSCs) younger than 30 million years old in the Local System was studied. It was shown for the first time that a significant number of OSCs belong to the recently discovered Vela Ridge gas and dust supercloud. The most intriguing property of this sample of OSCs is the presence of periodic perturbations in their vertical coordinates with a maximum amplitude of 47 pc and a wavelength of 1.1 kpc. Thus, the discovered chain of young OSCs is analogous to the Radcliffe Wave, but with a lower amplitude of vertical perturbations, a shorter wavelength, and is, on average, 2 million years older.

AI.tldr: This paper studies open star clusters (OSCs) younger than 30 Myr in the Local System, revealing that many belong to the Vela Ridge supercloud and that they exhibit periodic vertical perturbations (amplitude 47 pc, wavelength 1.1 kpc) analogous to but distinct from the Radcliffe Wave.
AI.motivation: To understand the spatial distribution and vertical structure of young open star clusters in the Local System, particularly their association with recently discovered large-scale gas and dust structures like the Vela Ridge, and to identify patterns in their three-dimensional spatial arrangement.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of the spatial distribution of open star clusters younger than 30 Myr in the Local System, examining their association with the Vela Ridge supercloud and analyzing their vertical coordinate perturbations.
AI.result: A significant number of young OSCs belong to the Vela Ridge supercloud. The clusters exhibit periodic vertical perturbations with a maximum amplitude of 47 pc and wavelength of 1.1 kpc, forming a chain analogous to the Radcliffe Wave but with lower amplitude, shorter wavelength, and ~2 Myr older average age.
AI.conclusion: The discovered chain of young OSCs represents a new coherent structure in the Galactic plane—a smaller-scale, older analog of the Radcliffe Wave—revealing that similar wave-like vertical perturbations exist at different scales and ages in the local interstellar medium.
